idea.why: Genuine multi-agent decomposition: two analyst agents own one source each, a third editor agent cross-references and prioritises. The model emits only a semantic fragment and a deterministic template supplies the chrome, so the layout cannot drift day to day. Debatable call: treating dashboard as an emailed document rather than a page with a URL.

structure.why: Node types fit their jobs and nine functional nodes is proportionate, with no Set or Code ceremony. Small mismatch: the editor agent has no tools and is a pure text transform, work a Basic LLM Chain does with less machinery.

connections.why: Calendar Agent waits on Email Triage Agent despite consuming nothing from it; the editor reaches both by node reference, so the chain is execution-order accident, not data flow. An empty email branch silently starves the calendar branch and the whole briefing.

answer.why: A reader of the brief would recognise their request: daily run over both sources, information actually sorted, rendered as a responsive card grid, delivered to the inbox. Falls short of a literal dashboard only in that nothing is hosted; the HTML exists solely as an email body.

appraisal: This finds a sensible shape rather than the first one that compiles: source-specific analyst agents, a separate editor that merges and prioritises, and a clean split between generated content and a deterministic styled shell so the dashboard looks the same every morning. Prompt-level guardrails against invented senders and deadlines. The flaw is the wiring: the two agents are strictly independent yet run in a chain, which buys nothing, misrepresents the dependency graph, and lets an empty inbox take the calendar down with it. A knowledgeable user would fan both out from the trigger and rejoin at a Merge, then downgrade the toolless editor to a Basic LLM Chain, and optionally hang a Webhook off the HTML node so the briefing has a URL.
